From brazë.

ety.text: From Proto-Albanian *dranga. Cognate with Old Norse drangr (“stone pillar”), Lithuanian dránga (“perch, pole”), Proto-Slavic *drǫgъ.
From *drenk(ë), derivative of dre (“deer”) + -kë (diminutive suffix).
Univerbation of gjysa mi gjysa zog, literally “half mouse half bird”. Compare the synonymous gjysmami and gjysmazog.
From Proto-Albanian *graska or *grah, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷr̥H-sḱé-ti, from *gʷerH- (“to raise a cry”). Frequently ngrah with the intensive prefix n-.

ety.text: From kaca- + gjel (“rooster, cock”). Given that boastfulness is a characteristic usually ascribed to roosters rather than ants, it seems that noun sense 2 developed parallelly from the original meaning of gjel rather than from noun sense 1.

From kaca- + gjel (“rooster, cock”). Given that boastfulness is a characteristic usually ascribed to roosters rather than ants, it seems that noun sense 2 developed parallelly from the original meaning of gjel rather than from noun sense 1.
From Proto-Indo-European *ku̯ak (“croaking, quacking”). Compare Ancient Greek κοάξ (koáx, “frog's croak”), Latin coaxare (“to croak”) and Old Norse kvaka (“chirp, twitter”).

ety.text: Possibly a devoiced variant of gungë + -ull, from Proto-Indo-European *geng-, *gong- (“lump”). Close to Lithuanian gungulỹs (“ball”), Old Norse kǫngull (“bundle of berries”), Ancient Greek γογγύλος (gongúlos, “round”), Latin conucla (“staff for holding flax, wool, etc.”). Alternatively from Proto-Albanian *kunkula, similar to Lithuanian kunkulas (“bubble”).

tpl.gloss: staff for holding flax, wool, etc.

ety.text: Attested as Ottoman Turkish [script needed] (lubesko, lupesko) [1431], Greek Λίουπτζκα (Líouptzka) [1857]. According to Ylli SLA, to be connected with Bulgarian лю́пя (ljúpja), лу́пя (lúpja, “to peel”), compare Macedonian лупешка (lupeška, “peel, outer covering”). Was proposed for renaming in 1938 as Rreminë.
From Proto-Albanian *lapā, a derivative of lapë. Cognate to Greek λοπός (lopós, “shell, husk, bark”), Lithuanian lãpas (“leaf”).

ety.text: From lëpushë (“mullein; coltsfoot”).

Unclear. It could be a borrowing from a South Slavic language, compare Serbo-Croatian morač (Svane). According to Çabej, it derives from Latin amaracus (“marjoram”). Another possibility is a borrowing from Vulgar Latin *marathrium, *marathricum, from Latin marathrum. See also Romanian mărar.
From Proto-Albanian *mata, from pre-Albanian *mn̥to, from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to tower, stand out”) (compare Welsh mynydd, Latin mōns, Avestan 𐬨𐬀𐬙𐬌 (mati)).

ety.text: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish اسكندر (iskender), from Classical Persian اسکندر (iskandar), from Arabic الْإِسْكَنْدَر (al-ʔiskandar), from Ancient Greek Ἀλέξανδρος (Aléxandros). Doublet of Aleksandër and Lleshdër. Cognate with Turkish İskender and Azerbaijani İsgəndər.

Derived from *ur. From Proto-Albanian *wana, a nominal derivative of Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to want, to desire”). Cognate to English wish, Latin venia (“indulgence, kindness”).
